## The idea

In D major, a written F sounds as F-sharp even when no sharp is printed beside
that particular note. The key signature supplies the standing rule. A natural
sign can override it locally, later Fs in the same bar inherit that override,
and the signature's F-sharp returns after the barline. What the page omits is as
important as what it marks explicitly.

A *key signature* maps letter names to default sharp or flat alterations. An
*accidental* supplies a local override, scoped here to one bar and one
letter-octave position. The notation behaves like nested configuration: a global
default, mutable state within the bar, and an optional assignment on the current
event. Resolving those layers in order prevents an unmarked note from being
mistaken for a natural.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 88
use_synth :piano

semitones = {c: 0, d: 2, e: 4, f: 5, g: 7, a: 9, b: 11}
key_signature = {f: 1, c: 1}  # D major

define :resolve_note do |event, key_signature, local, semitones|
  scope_key = [event[:letter], event[:octave]]
  local[scope_key] = event[:accidental] if event.key?(:accidental)
  alteration = local.fetch(scope_key, key_signature.fetch(event[:letter], 0))
  12 * (event[:octave] + 1) + semitones[event[:letter]] + alteration
end

bars = [
  [
    {letter: :f, octave: 4, duration: 1},
    {letter: :g, octave: 4, duration: 1},
    {letter: :f, octave: 4, duration: 1, accidental: 0},
    {letter: :f, octave: 4, duration: 1}
  ],
  [
    {letter: :f, octave: 4, duration: 1},
    {letter: :c, octave: 5, duration: 1},
    {letter: :c, octave: 5, duration: 1, accidental: -1},
    {letter: :d, octave: 5, duration: 1}
  ]
]

bars.each do |bar|
  local = {}
  bar.each do |event|
    pitch = resolve_note(event, key_signature, local, semitones)
    puts "#{event} -> #{pitch}"
    play pitch, release: 0.7
    sleep event[:duration]
  end
end
```

The first F inherits one sharp from the signature. The explicit natural stores
zero as the local F4 alteration, so the following F4 remains natural without
another sign. When the next bar creates a new `local` hash, F-sharp returns. The
C-flat example follows the same precedence in the other direction: an event can
replace a sharp default with a flat local value.

## Change one thing

1. Change the signature to `{b: -1, e: -1}` for B-flat major. Flats and sharps
   use negative and positive values in one alteration field, so the resolver
   needs no new control path.
2. Add F5 after the F4 natural. Because the local key includes octave, F5 still
   inherits F-sharp from the signature. Remove octave from `scope_key` and hear
   the F4 natural incorrectly spread into another register.
3. Add an explicit sharp after the natural in the same bar. The later sign
   replaces the earlier F4 assignment, demonstrating that local accidental state
   can change more than once before the barline resets it.

## Why it works

The resolver searches from the most local information outward. An accidental on
the current event first updates bar state. Existing bar state takes precedence
over the key signature, and the signature takes precedence over the table of
natural pitch classes. Nested `fetch` calls make that fallback order visible in
the code rather than relying on a collection of special cases.

Letter and alteration remain separate through the calculation. F-sharp and
G-flat can resolve to the same MIDI number while preserving different source
letters and signs. That difference supports correct interval names, key-aware
analysis, and faithful comparison with a printed edition. Collapsing both notes
to pitch class 6 too early would make later reconstruction guesswork.

Published notation includes rules beyond this example, among them conventions
for cancelling accidentals and special treatment of notes tied across a barline.
The current resolver states a smaller model and exposes its boundary. Extend it
when a real source supplies a case the model cannot express, so each new branch
answers an observed notation problem rather than a speculative one.

Key signatures store defaults by letter, which brings the circle of fifths back
into the data model. D major sharpens F and C; it does not announce anonymous
pitch classes 6 and 1. A G-flat in the same passage reaches the same MIDI key as
F-sharp through a different spelling. Preserve the written letter after
resolution so a diagnostic can distinguish deliberate enharmonic spelling from
an encoding error.

## Take it further

Write `resolve_bar(events, key_signature)` so it returns new hashes with a MIDI
`:note` while preserving letter, octave, start, duration, and any accidental.
Use a four-bar phrase containing a sharp signature, a natural override, a
repeated affected note, the same letter in another octave, and a barline reset.
Print each source event beside its resolved form. The paired output should show
both what the notation said and which layer supplied the final alteration.
